title: Choosing a Framework

techniques.name: A Plain SDK Loop
techniques.q: Do I need a framework at all?
techniques.what: An agent is a loop: call the model with tools, run the tools it asks for, send back the results, stop when it answers. With a provider SDK that is about 45 lines, with nothing hidden and no framework to upgrade. You then own everything else: retries, saving state, pausing for approval and resuming, tracing, streaming and parallel tool calls. Many production agents stay this simple; start here and adopt a framework when a specific need appears.

Simple agents with a few tools
Teams that want full control and few dependencies
metrics: call, run tools, append results, repeat
a step limit so it cannot loop forever
saving and resuming, if runs are long

steps: Write the loop with a step budget
Add tools with clear schemas (Tools & MCP)
Gate risky tools behind approval
Add persistence and tracing only when needed
pitfalls: Rebuilding a framework badly, one feature at a time
No step budget
Blocking a web request while waiting for a human
techniques.remember: Start with the loop; adopt a framework for a need, not a trend.

techniques.name: Pydantic AI
techniques.q: How do I get typed, validated agents with little ceremony?
techniques.what: Pydantic AI, from the team behind Pydantic, defines an agent with a model, typed dependencies and a typed output. Tool arguments and final outputs are validated Pydantic models, and invalid output goes back to the model for a retry. It supports most providers through one API, injects dependencies such as a bank client so agents are easy to test, and integrates with Temporal, DBOS and Prefect for durable runs, with Logfire for tracing.

Agents that must return structured data
Model-agnostic apps that may switch providers
metrics: a Pydantic model the answer must match
Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock and more
steps: Define the output model and dependencies
Register tools with typed arguments
Run with injected dependencies; test with fakes
Add durable execution for long runs
pitfalls: Assuming validation means correct values (Prompting & Structured Outputs)
Putting business state in globals instead of deps
Expecting built-in multi-agent teams
techniques.remember: Type the output, inject the dependencies, validate everything.

techniques.name: LangGraph
techniques.q: How do I build long-running agents that pause, resume and survive crashes?
techniques.what: LangGraph models an agent as a graph of nodes that read and write shared state. A checkpointer saves state after every step for each thread, so a run can pause for human approval with interrupt(), survive a crash, and resume hours later; you can also inspect and replay past steps. LangChain’s create_agent builds the common loop on top. It is the most explicit option for durable, controllable workflows, at the cost of more concepts to learn.
use: Long-running cases with human approvals
Workflows needing precise control of each step
Teams that want replay and time-travel debugging
metrics: nodes and edges over shared state
pause for a human; resume with Command
steps: Start from create_agent with your tools
Add a Postgres checkpointer and a thread per case
Put interrupt() before risky actions
Move to a custom graph when you need explicit control
pitfalls: Using the in-memory checkpointer in production
Graphs more complex than the problem
Side effects that repeat on resume
techniques.remember: State per thread, a checkpoint per step, interrupt before risk.

techniques.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
techniques.q: How do I build agents that hand off to each other, with guardrails, quickly?
techniques.what: The OpenAI Agents SDK is a small set of primitives: agents with instructions and tools, a runner that executes the loop, handoffs that pass a conversation to a specialist agent, guardrails that run alongside and can stop a run, sessions for memory, and built-in tracing. Recent additions include sandbox agents, realtime voice agents and human approval. It works with other providers through LiteLLM but fits OpenAI models best.
use: Triage-and-specialist designs
Teams already on OpenAI models
Fast prototypes that still need guardrails and traces
metrics: input and output checks with tripwires
steps: Define specialist agents with tools
Add a triage agent with handoffs
Add input and output guardrails
Use sessions and read the traces
pitfalls: Handoff chains that bounce between agents
Relying on guardrails as the only safety layer
Assuming non-OpenAI models behave identically
techniques.remember: Triage, hand off, guard the edges, trace everything.

techniques.name: Claude Agent SDK
techniques.q: How do I build an autonomous agent that works with files, code and tools?
techniques.what: The Claude Agent SDK gives you the agent harness behind Claude Code as a library: built-in tools for files, shell and the web, context management, subagents, sessions, hooks that run before and after tool calls, and permission modes. Your own tools are added as MCP servers, including in-process ones. It runs Claude models only, and it is strongest for autonomous work such as operations, research and coding tasks where the agent needs a workspace.

Operations and research agents
Teams standardising on Claude models
metrics: Read, Write, Bash, WebFetch and more
steps: Expose your tools through an MCP server

pitfalls: Granting Bash and write access by default

techniques.remember: A full harness: allow little, hook the risky calls, sandbox the rest.
techniques.cap: Claude models only; Python and TypeScript.

techniques.name: Google Agent Development Kit
techniques.q: How do I compose agents and workflows across languages, especially on Google Cloud?
techniques.what: Google’s Agent Development Kit builds LLM agents and composes them with workflow agents that run sub-agents in sequence, in parallel or in a loop, with graph workflows added in ADK 2.0. A runner and session service manage state and events. It supports Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin, works with Gemini and other models, includes a web UI and evaluation tooling, speaks A2A, and deploys naturally to Cloud Run or Google’s agent runtime.
use: Teams on Google Cloud or using Gemini
Java, Go or Kotlin shops
Multi-agent systems that talk A2A
steps: Build an LlmAgent with tools
Compose steps with workflow agents
Test with adk web and adk eval
Deploy to Cloud Run or the managed runtime
pitfalls: Assuming every feature is equal across languages
Tying deployment to one cloud without meaning to
Nesting workflow agents deeper than needed
tools: Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise agent runtime
techniques.remember: LLM agents inside workflow agents, in the language you already use.

techniques.name: CrewAI, AutoGen and Microsoft Agent Framework
techniques.q: When do I want a team of role-based agents?
techniques.what: CrewAI defines agents by role, goal and backstory, assigns them tasks and runs them as a crew, sequentially or under a manager agent, with Flows for event-driven control. AutoGen pioneered conversational multi-agent systems; Microsoft moved it to maintenance in October 2025, and its successor, Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 (April 2026), merges AutoGen and Semantic Kernel for .NET and Python. AG2 continues AutoGen as a community project. Teams of agents fit genuinely parallel, separable work, and cost several times the tokens (Multi-Agent Systems).
use: Research and content pipelines with separable roles
.NET and Azure shops (Microsoft Agent Framework)
Prototyping multi-agent designs quickly
steps: Check that the work really splits into roles (Multi-Agent Systems)
Define agents and tasks with expected outputs
Start sequential; add a manager only if needed
Measure tokens and consistency against one agent
pitfalls: Role-play prompts instead of clear tasks
Starting new work on AutoGen
Multi-agent cost for single-agent problems
techniques.remember: Teams only for work that truly divides; mind the token bill.
techniques.cap: Microsoft Agent Framework for .NET; CrewAI for Python.

techniques.name: TypeScript Agents: Vercel AI SDK and Mastra
techniques.q: How do I build agents in TypeScript, next to my web app?
techniques.what: Many product teams work in TypeScript, and their agents live inside Next.js or Node services. The Vercel AI SDK is the common base: generateText and streamText run the tool loop with a step limit, tools are defined with Zod schemas, streaming UI hooks such as useChat render tokens and tool calls, and one line switches between model providers. Mastra builds on it with agents, workflows that can suspend for a human and resume later from storage, memory, RAG helpers and evals. LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK and Google ADK also have TypeScript versions; this tab is for teams who want a TypeScript-first stack.

Streaming chat and generative UI in the browser
Teams that want to switch model providers freely

pitfalls: Running long agent loops inside a serverless request with a short timeout
Blocking a request for a human approval that may take hours
Trusting Zod validation as proof the arguments are correct
techniques.remember: Zod-typed tools, a step limit, stream to the UI; Mastra when runs must pause.

cmp.best: Long runs inside short request timeouts

techniques.name: LlamaIndex
techniques.q: How do I build agents that are mostly about my documents?
techniques.what: LlamaIndex started as a data framework for RAG and is strongest when an agent’s job is mostly about documents: readers for hundreds of sources, LlamaParse for complex PDFs, indexes and query engines that turn retrieval into a tool. On top sit FunctionAgent and AgentWorkflow for single and multi-agent loops, and Workflows, an event-driven way to write steps whose Context can be serialised and resumed, including waiting for human input. It runs in Python and TypeScript. The RAG techniques themselves (parsing, chunking, re-ranking, citations) are covered in module 18; this tab is about LlamaIndex as a framework.

Policy, compliance and research assistants
Teams already using LlamaIndex for RAG
metrics: load PDFs, Drive, Confluence and more; parse tables and layouts
VectorStoreIndex, retrievers, re-rankers behind one query call

steps: Load and parse documents; build an index and query engine
Wrap the query engine and business functions as tools

pitfalls: Default chunking and top-k left untuned on complex PDFs
Using the framework’s agent layer when a plain loop plus its retrievers would do
Upgrading across versions without pinning; APIs have moved often
techniques.remember: Documents in, query engines as tools, Context you can save.

TOOLS = [{"name": "get_transaction", ...},                              #@1
         {"name": "raise_dispute", ...}]                                  #@1

def run_tool(name, args):
    if name == "raise_dispute" and not approvals.request(**args):        #@4
        return "Rejected by reviewer."                                   #@4
    return FUNCS[name](**args)

def agent(question, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):                          # step budget     #@2
        r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, system=SYSTEM,           #@2
                                   tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)       #@2
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        if r.stop_reason != "tool_use":                                  #@3
            return text_of(r)                                            #@3
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [                   #@3
            tool_result(b.id, run_tool(b.name, b.input))                 #@3
            for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]})                #@3
    raise RuntimeError("step budget exhausted")                          #@5
# persistence, resume, tracing, streaming: yours to add                  #@6
steps: Describe the tools
Two tools with JSON schemas: look up a transaction by UTR, and raise a dispute. Good descriptions matter more than any framework (Tools & MCP).
Call the model inside a budget
The loop sends the conversation and the tools. The step budget stops a confused agent from looping forever.
Run the tools it asks for
If the model stopped to use tools, run them and send back the results; otherwise its text is the answer. That is the whole agent.
Gate the risky tool
A person approves before a dispute is raised. In a plain loop this blocks; that is fine for minutes, not for days.
Fail loudly
If the budget runs out, raise an error rather than returning half an answer.
Know what you now own
About 30 lines, no framework to upgrade. Persistence, resume, tracing, streaming and parallel calls are yours to write if you need them.

class Reply(BaseModel):                                                  #@1
    status: Literal["succeeded", "dispute_raised", "rejected", "not_found"]   #@1
    message: str                                                          #@1

agent = Agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",                              #@5
              deps_type=Bank, output_type=Reply,                          #@2
              instructions=SYSTEM)

@agent.tool                                                               #@3
async def get_transaction(ctx: RunContext[Bank], utr: str) -> dict:      #@3
    return await ctx.deps.transactions.get(utr)                          #@3

@agent.tool
async def raise_dispute(ctx: RunContext[Bank], utr: str, reason: str):
    if not await ctx.deps.approvals.request(utr, reason):                 #@4
        return "Rejected by reviewer."                                   #@4
    return await ctx.deps.disputes.create(utr, reason)

result = agent.run_sync(QUESTION, deps=bank)                              #@6
print(result.output.status)                  # a validated Reply          #@6
steps: Type the answer
Reply is a Pydantic model with a fixed set of statuses. Downstream code can switch on status without parsing text.
Declare dependencies
deps_type=Bank says what every run receives. Tools use ctx.deps instead of globals, so tests pass a fake bank.
Typed tools
Arguments are validated before the tool runs; the schema is generated from the type hints and docstring.
Approval through the dependency
The approval service is part of the injected bank, so a test can approve or reject automatically.
Any provider, one string
Switching from Anthropic to OpenAI or Google is a change to the model string, not a rewrite.
A validated result
result.output is a Reply. If the model returns something invalid, Pydantic AI sends the error back and retries.

@tool
def raise_dispute(utr: str, reason: str) -> str:
    """Raise a dispute for a failed UPI debit."""
    decision = interrupt({"utr": utr, "reason": reason})     # pause      #@3
    if decision != "approve":                                            #@5
        return "Rejected by reviewer."                                   #@5
    return bank.disputes.create(utr, reason)       # after approval only  #@5

with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URL) as saver:                    #@2
    agent = create_agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",                  #@1
                         tools=[get_transaction, raise_dispute],         #@1
                         system_prompt=SYSTEM, checkpointer=saver)       #@2
    case = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "case-8812"}}                  #@2
    agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": Q}]}, case)   #@3

    # hours later, another process                                       #@4
    agent.invoke(Command(resume="approve"), case)                        #@4
# inspect or replay: agent.get_state_history(case)                       #@6
steps: The standard loop, prebuilt
create_agent builds the model-and-tools loop as a LangGraph graph. Custom graphs come later, if ever.
A checkpointer and a thread per case
Postgres stores the state after every step under thread_id case-8812. The in-memory saver is for tests only.
interrupt() pauses the run
Inside the tool, interrupt() stops the run and saves it. The request returns; nothing waits in memory.
Resume from anywhere, any time
A different process, two days later, resumes the same thread with Command(resume="approve").
Side effects after the pause
On resume the tool runs again from its start, so the dispute is created only after the decision and must be idempotent.
Replay and inspect
Every step is saved, so you can list the history, inspect state and replay from a past checkpoint when debugging.

def get_transaction(utr: str) -> dict:                                  #@1
    """Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR."""                 #@1
    return bank.transactions.get(utr)                                    #@1

@input_guardrail                                                         #@3
async def no_card_numbers(ctx, agent, user_input):                       #@3
    found = bool(CARD.search(str(user_input)))                           #@3
    return GuardrailFunctionOutput(output_info={"card": found},          #@3
                                   tripwire_triggered=found)             #@3

disputes = Agent(name="Disputes", instructions=SYSTEM,                   #@2
                 tools=[get_transaction, raise_dispute])                  #@2
triage = Agent(name="Triage", model="gpt-5-mini",                        #@2
               handoffs=[disputes], input_guardrails=[no_card_numbers])  #@2

session = SQLiteSession("customer-4471")                                  #@4
result = Runner.run_sync(triage, QUESTION, session=session)               #@5
print(result.final_output)                  # traces recorded by default #@6
steps: Tools from functions
function_tool turns a typed Python function and its docstring into a tool schema.
Triage hands off
A cheap triage agent answers simple questions and hands failed payments to the Disputes agent, which then talks to the customer directly.
A guardrail with a tripwire
The input guardrail runs alongside the agent. A pasted card number trips it and stops the run with an exception you catch.
Sessions remember
SQLiteSession keeps the customer’s conversation, so the next message continues it.
Run the loop
Runner executes the agents, tools and handoffs until there is a final output.
Read the traces
Tracing is on by default. Here traces showed 30% of chats handed off, which set the specialist’s cost.

async def require_approval(input_data, tool_use_id, context):             #@3

        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",     #@3
                "permissionDecision": "deny"}}                           #@3
    return {}

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(

    allowed_tools=["mcp__bank__get_transaction",                          #@2
                   "mcp__bank__raise_dispute"],                           #@2
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="mcp__bank__raise_dispute", #@3
                                      hooks=[require_approval])]},        #@3
    max_turns=8)                                                          #@4

async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=options) as client:                    #@5

steps: Your tools as an MCP server
The bank tools are served by an in-process MCP server, the same protocol used for external tools (Tools & MCP).
Allow only what the task needs
Only the two bank tools are allowed. The built-in Read, Write and Bash tools exist but are not granted to this agent.
A hook gates the risky call
A PreToolUse hook on raise_dispute asks for approval and denies the call if the reviewer rejects it.
Limit the turns
max_turns caps the loop, the same idea as a step budget.
A session with the harness
ClaudeSDKClient runs a multi-turn session with Claude Code’s context management underneath.
Stream the messages
Messages stream back as they happen: text, tool calls and results, which you can log or show.

def get_transaction(utr: str) -> dict:                                    #@1
    """Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR."""                  #@1
    return bank.transactions.get(utr)                                     #@1

agent = Agent(name="upi_disputes", model="gemini-flash-latest",           #@2
              instruction=SYSTEM,                                         #@2
              tools=[get_transaction, raise_dispute])                     #@2

runner = Runner(agent=agent, app_name="support",                          #@3
                session_service=InMemorySessionService())                 #@3

async def ask(user_id, question):
    session = await runner.session_service.create_session(                #@3
        app_name="support", user_id=user_id)                              #@3
    message = types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part(text=question)])
    async for event in runner.run_async(user_id=user_id,                  #@4
                                        session_id=session.id,            #@4
                                        new_message=message):             #@4
        if event.is_final_response():                                     #@4
            return event.content.parts[0].text                            #@4

An LLM agent
Name, model, instruction and tools. Gemini by default; other models through adapters.
A runner and a session
The runner executes the agent; the session service stores state and events per user. Use a persistent one in production.
Events stream back
run_async yields events: model output, tool calls, results, and a final response.
Compose with workflow agents
Sequential, parallel and loop agents arrange LLM agents into a pipeline: here, three checks run in parallel.
Test, run and connect
adk eval tests behaviour, adk web gives a dev UI, and A2A lets these agents call agents in other frameworks.

steps: Agents as roles
Each agent has a role, a goal and a backstory, and only the tools its role needs.
Tasks with expected outputs
Clear tasks with expected outputs matter more than colourful backstories.
A human reviews
human_input=True asks a person to review the task’s result before it is final.
Run the crew
A sequential process runs the tasks in order, passing results along. A hierarchical process adds a manager agent.
Measure against one agent
For this support case the crew used 3.6 times the tokens of a single agent with no accuracy gain.

steps: One package for the loop
The ai package runs the model, the tools and the loop. Provider packages plug in underneath.
Tools with Zod schemas
Each tool has a description, a Zod input schema and an execute function. The schema becomes the JSON schema the model sees, and arguments are validated before execute runs.
A bounded loop
generateText keeps calling tools until the model answers or stopWhen ends it: here at 8 steps.
Gate the risky tool
This approval blocks the call. For approvals that take hours, a Mastra workflow suspends the run, stores its state and resumes when the reviewer answers.
Switch providers in one line
Swap anthropic() for openai() or google(); the tools and loop stay the same.
Stream it to users
In a Next.js route, streamText plus the useChat hook shows tokens and tool calls as they happen. About 24 lines for the same agent.

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext

class Reply(BaseModel):
    status: Literal["succeeded", "dispute_raised", "rejected", "not_found"]
    message: str

    "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",          # or "openai:...", "google-gla:..."
    deps_type=Bank,
    output_type=Reply,
    instructions=SYSTEM,
)

@agent.tool
async def get_transaction(ctx: RunContext[Bank], utr: str) -> dict:
    """Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR."""
    return await ctx.deps.transactions.get(utr)

@agent.tool
async def raise_dispute(ctx: RunContext[Bank], utr: str, reason: str) -> str:
    """Raise a dispute for a failed UPI debit. Needs human approval."""
    if not await ctx.deps.approvals.request(utr, reason):
        return "Rejected by reviewer."
    return await ctx.deps.disputes.create(utr, reason)

result = agent.run_sync("My ₹1,200 UPI payment failed but money was debited. UTR 412345678901",
                        deps=bank)

import json
from claude_agent_sdk import (ClaudeAgentOptions, ClaudeSDKClient, HookMatcher,
                              create_sdk_mcp_server, tool)

@tool("get_transaction", "Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR", {"utr": str})
async def get_transaction(args):
    txn = await bank.transactions.get(args["utr"])
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(txn)}]}

@tool("raise_dispute", "Raise a dispute for a failed UPI debit", {"utr": str, "reason": str})
async def raise_dispute(args):
    ref = await bank.disputes.create(args["utr"], args["reason"])
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"Dispute {ref} raised"}]}

async def require_approval(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    if not await approvals.request(input_data["tool_input"]):
        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
                "permissionDecision": "deny",
                "permissionDecisionReason": "Reviewer rejected the dispute"}}
    return {}

bank_server = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="bank", version="1.0.0",
                                    tools=[get_transaction, raise_dispute])
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt=SYSTEM,
    mcp_servers={"bank": bank_server},
    allowed_tools=["mcp__bank__get_transaction", "mcp__bank__raise_dispute"],
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="mcp__bank__raise_dispute",
                                      hooks=[require_approval])]},
    max_turns=8)

async def main():
    async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=options) as client:
        await client.query(QUESTION)
        async for message in client.receive_response():
            print(message)

from crewai import Agent, Crew, Process, Task
from crewai.tools import tool

@tool("Get transaction")
def get_transaction(utr: str) -> str:
    """Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR."""
    return str(bank.transactions.get(utr))

investigator = Agent(
    role="Payments investigator",
    goal="Find out what happened to the customer's UPI debit",
    backstory="You check transaction records and never guess.",
    tools=[get_transaction], llm="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5")

writer = Agent(
    role="Support writer",
    goal="Explain the outcome clearly and say what happens next",
    backstory="You write short, plain replies for customers.",
    llm="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5")

investigate = Task(description="Investigate UTR {utr}. Customer says: {question}",
                   expected_output="Status of the payment, with evidence", agent=investigator)
reply = Task(description="Write the reply. If a dispute is needed, say it is sent for approval.",
             expected_output="A reply of at most four sentences", agent=writer,
             human_input=True)                                 # a person reviews

            process=Process.sequential)

import asyncio
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool
from llama_index.llms.anthropic import Anthropic

docs = SimpleDirectoryReader("npci_upi_circulars/").load_data()
rules = QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(
    VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs).as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=4),
    name="upi_rules", description="NPCI and RBI rules on failed UPI payments")

def get_transaction(utr: str) -> dict:
    """Look up a UPI transaction by its 12-digit UTR."""
    return {"utr": utr, "status": "debited_not_credited", "amount": 2450, "days_since": 3}

agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[rules, get_transaction], llm=Anthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5"),
                      system_prompt="Help with failed UPI payments; cite the rule you rely on.")

async def main():
    print(await agent.run("My UTR 417803921556 payment failed 3 days ago. When is my refund due?"))
asyncio.run(main())

plain.title: The agent loop
plain.explain: There is no step budget. A model that keeps calling tools, or two tools that keep failing, loops forever and runs up the bill. Cap the iterations and raise when the cap is hit.
plain.fix: for _ in range(8):          # step budget; raise RuntimeError after the loop

also.5: Correct: stop when the model no longer asks for tools.

pydantic.title: A Pydantic AI tool
pydantic.explain: The tool ignores the injected dependency and calls a global production client. Tests cannot swap in a fake bank, and every test run hits production.

langgraph.title: Pausing for approval
langgraph.explain: The dispute is created before the human decides, and when the run resumes the tool runs again from its start, creating a second dispute. Side effects belong after interrupt(), and must be idempotent.
langgraph.fix: decision = interrupt({"utr": utr, "reason": reason})   # then create only if approved

also.5: Interrupt is the right mechanism; its position is the problem.

openai.title: The card-number guardrail

also.3: Correct: search the input for a card-like number.

claude.title: Agent options
claude.code:
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt=SYSTEM,
    mcp_servers={"bank": bank_server},
    permission_mode="bypassPermissions",
    max_turns=8)
claude.explain: Bypassing permissions lets every available tool run without checks, including the built-in shell and file-writing tools this dispute agent never needs. List the allowed tools explicitly and keep the default permission mode.

also.5: Correct: a turn limit, like a step budget.

adk.title: Composing the intake pipeline
adk.code:
intake = SequentialAgent(name="intake", sub_agents=[
    load_documents,
    ParallelAgent(name="checks", sub_agents=[extract_fields, check_policy, fraud_score]),
    summarise,
])
adk.explain: check_policy and fraud_score need the fields that extract_fields produces, but all three run in parallel, so the checks see no fields. Only independent steps belong in a ParallelAgent.

plain.q: Do we need an agent framework? How would you decide?
plain.model: Start with a plain loop on the provider SDK: it is short, transparent and has no framework upgrades. Adopt a framework when a concrete need appears that it solves well, such as durable state for multi-day cases, human approvals that wait hours, or genuine multi-agent orchestration, and weigh the learning curve and dependency it brings.

plain.q: What must every hand-written agent loop include?
plain.model: A step budget so it cannot run forever, tool errors returned to the model rather than crashing, an approval gate before risky actions, and tracing of every model and tool call so behaviour can be inspected.

plain.q: How do you avoid lock-in whatever you choose?
plain.model: Write tools once as MCP servers so any framework can use them, keep business logic outside framework-specific code behind a thin interface, and keep an eval suite that lets you compare a replacement objectively.

pydantic.q: What does Pydantic AI give over a plain SDK?
pydantic.model: Typed, validated outputs with automatic retries, typed tool arguments, dependency injection that makes agents testable, one API across most providers, and integrations for durable execution, tracing and evals.

pydantic.q: How would you test a Pydantic AI agent?
pydantic.model: Inject a fake bank through deps, use a test model that returns scripted responses to check the logic without calling a provider, and run evals with real models on labelled cases before release.

pydantic.q: Does a validated output mean a correct one?
pydantic.model: No. Validation guarantees the shape: fields and types. The values can still be wrong, so business rules such as matching totals or valid references must still be checked in code.

langgraph.q: How does LangGraph handle human approval in a long-running case?
langgraph.model: A node or tool calls interrupt() with what the reviewer needs. The run stops and the checkpointer saves its state under the case’s thread id. Hours or days later, any process resumes the thread with Command(resume=...) carrying the decision.

langgraph.q: What goes wrong with side effects around interrupts?
langgraph.model: When resumed, the interrupted node or tool runs again from its start, so anything before interrupt() executes twice. Put side effects after the decision and make them idempotent, for example with a key per case.

For short, simple tool loops that never pause or need replay. Its concepts, state, nodes, reducers and checkpointers, are worth learning when durability and control are real needs, not for a two-tool chat agent.

openai.q: Explain handoffs and guardrails in the OpenAI Agents SDK.
openai.model: A handoff transfers the conversation to another agent, which then answers the user directly; it suits triage to specialists. Guardrails run on the first agent’s input or the last agent’s output and can trip a wire that stops the run. Tracing records every step by default.

openai.q: Handoff or agent-as-tool: how do you choose?
openai.model: Use a handoff when a specialist should take over the conversation, as in routing. Call an agent as a tool when the first agent should stay in charge, get the sub-agent’s result back and continue.

openai.q: What are the limits of SDK guardrails for safety?
openai.model: They are one layer: checks at the edges of a run. Real safety also needs narrow tool permissions, approval gates before irreversible actions, and monitoring, as in the Guardrails and Agent Security modules.

claude.q: When would you choose the Claude Agent SDK?
claude.model: When the agent needs a workspace, reading and writing files, running code or a shell, browsing, over long contexts, as in operations, research or coding. It provides the Claude Code harness with those tools, hooks, permissions, subagents and sessions, but runs only Claude models.

claude.q: How do you make an agent with shell access safe?
claude.model: Allow only the tools the task needs, gate risky calls with PreToolUse hooks or approval, avoid bypassing permissions, run in a sandboxed container without production credentials, cap turns, and log every tool call.

claude.q: How do your own tools plug into the Claude Agent SDK?
claude.model: As MCP servers: external ones, or in-process servers created with create_sdk_mcp_server from decorated Python functions, which avoid a separate process. The same tools can serve other MCP-capable frameworks.

adk.q: What are ADK’s workflow agents and when do you use them?
adk.model: Workflow agents orchestrate sub-agents without calling a model themselves: SequentialAgent runs them in order, ParallelAgent runs independent ones at once, and LoopAgent repeats until a condition is met. They give deterministic structure around LLM agents.

adk.q: Why might a Java-based bank choose ADK?
adk.model: ADK supports Java and Go as well as Python and TypeScript, so agents can live inside existing services. It speaks A2A for cross-framework calls and deploys naturally on Google Cloud, with Gemini and other models.

adk.q: What is the risk with ParallelAgent?
adk.model: Running steps in parallel that depend on each other’s output, or that write the same state, gives wrong or racy results. Parallelise only independent checks and join their results afterwards.

crew.q: When is a crew of agents the right design?
crew.model: When the work genuinely divides into roles or parallel parts with clear hand-offs, such as research, analysis and writing. Crews cost several times the tokens of one agent, so measure accuracy and cost against a single agent before committing.

crew.q: What is the status of AutoGen, and what should a .NET team use?
crew.model: AutoGen moved to maintenance mode in October 2025. Microsoft Agent Framework, its successor, reached 1.0 in April 2026 and merges AutoGen with Semantic Kernel for .NET and Python, so a .NET team should use it; AG2 continues AutoGen as a community project.

crew.q: How do you keep a CrewAI system reliable?
crew.model: Write clear tasks with expected outputs rather than relying on role-play, start with a sequential process, wrap crews in Flows for state and control, add human review on outputs that matter, and track tokens and consistency.

tsagents.q: How would you build an agent in a TypeScript web product?
tsagents.model: Define tools with Zod in the Vercel AI SDK, run streamText with a step limit in a route, stream to the UI with useChat, and put long approvals in a Mastra workflow that suspends and resumes.

tsagents.q: 8 steps at 1.2 s each: worst case?

llamaindex.q: When is LlamaIndex a good fit for an agent?
llamaindex.model: When the agent’s work is mostly about documents: LlamaIndex loads and parses them, builds indexes and query engines that become agent tools, and offers Workflows with resumable Context for long cases.

llamaindex.q: 4 × 512-token chunks plus 1,200 tokens of prompt: input tokens?

cases.title: Choosing a framework for the collections agent
cases.brief: Kosha Finance, an NBFC, is building an agent to run loan-collection cases: review payment history, propose a restructuring or a reminder, and draft messages to borrowers. A vendor has pitched a six-agent crew - negotiator, analyst, compliance officer, writer, scheduler and a manager. An engineer's weekend prototype on the Claude Agent SDK works, with Bash and Write enabled. The CTO wants to know what to use and in what order to decide.
evidence: Cases last three to ten days. Nothing may be sent to a borrower without a credit officer's approval, and servers are redeployed several times a week.
The team is four Python engineers. None has run an agent framework in production, and a first version has to ship in six weeks.
Board policy requires the ability to change model provider within a quarter, and every outbound message must be a validated structured object before it is queued.
In the prototype, a restarted server re-sends a borrower reminder that had already gone out, because the side effect sits inside the step that resumes.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.plain: Start here, and the point is that the answer is no - which you only earn by asking. Four engineers with no production framework experience and six weeks should reach for the smallest thing that works, and for many agents a plain loop is it. Here it is not: cases pause for days awaiting a credit officer while servers redeploy several times a week, and building durable pause-and-resume yourself is this technique's first pitfall - rebuilding a framework badly, one feature at a time. Write down why you are not using a plain loop, because the next agent this team builds probably should.
why.langgraph: The requirement that decides everything is in symptom 1: a case that lives for ten days with a human approval in the middle, on servers redeployed weekly. That is durable execution with checkpointing, and it is what LangGraph is for. Two pitfalls matter immediately - use a real checkpointer rather than the in-memory one, and move the send outside the resumable step, which is symptom 4 exactly. Keep the graph no more complex than the problem.
why.pydantic: Two requirements point here: a validated structured object for every outbound message, and the board's demand to change provider within a quarter, which is what a model-agnostic typed layer buys you. Remember that validation proves shape and not truth - a well-formed message to the wrong borrower still validates - and keep case state in dependencies rather than globals.
why.claude: Useful for a different job than this one: it suits agents that read and write files, run code or use a shell, so it is a good fit for the team's internal tooling. The weekend prototype is also a warning rather than a recommendation - Bash and Write enabled by default is its named pitfall, and it offers nothing for a ten-day pause across redeploys.
why.llamaindex: Useful later: if the agent grows into answering questions over loan agreements and RBI circulars, its retrievers are the right layer. Nothing in this evidence is document-heavy yet.
why.openai: Not needed: the design is one agent with a human approval, not triage-and-specialist handoffs - and leaning on a provider's SDK sits awkwardly with a board policy about switching providers within a quarter.
why.adk: Not needed: this is a four-person Python team with no Google Cloud or Gemini requirement and no multi-language or A2A need. It would tie deployment to one cloud for no gain here.
why.crew: Not needed, and this is the vendor pitch to refuse. Six role-played agents for a single sequential case is multi-agent cost for a single-agent problem, and role-play prompts instead of clear tasks is the first pitfall. There is one case, one decision and one approval.
why.tsagents: Not needed: the team is four Python engineers and there is no web product to embed the agent in.

firstWhy.langgraph: The right answer and your second step - the ten-day pause across weekly redeploys genuinely requires durable checkpointing. But reach for it with the reason written down, because a team that adopts a graph framework without first asking whether a loop would do tends to build graphs more complex than the problem, which is one of its own pitfalls.
firstWhy.pydantic: Both of its requirements are real - validated outbound messages and provider portability within a quarter - and you will use it. But it is a layer inside whatever runs the case, and what runs the case is the open question: a typed agent that loses its state on Tuesday's redeploy is still broken.
firstWhy.claude: The prototype works, which is seductive with six weeks on the clock. But it works on a weekend task, not on a ten-day case that must survive redeploys - and it is running with Bash and Write enabled, which is the one configuration its own documentation warns against. Promising prototypes are not architecture decisions.

cases.model: Start by asking whether a framework is needed at all, and record the answer: with four engineers new to agent frameworks and six weeks to ship, the smallest thing that works is the right instinct - but cases here pause for days awaiting a credit officer while servers redeploy weekly, and hand-rolling durable pause-and-resume is how teams rebuild a framework badly one feature at a time. So the answer is no, for a stated reason the next project can re-examine. Then adopt LangGraph for the durable execution that requirement implies: a real checkpointer rather than the in-memory one, side effects moved outside the resumable step so a restart cannot re-send a reminder, and a graph no more elaborate than the case actually is. Use Pydantic AI inside it for the validated outbound message objects and for the provider portability the board requires, keeping case state in dependencies and remembering that validation proves shape rather than correctness. Keep the Claude Agent SDK in mind for internal file-and-shell tooling, with Bash and Write off by default, and LlamaIndex for later if document questions grow. Refuse the six-agent crew: one sequential case with one approval is a single-agent problem, and role-played specialists would add cost and bouncing for nothing.
cases.note: The first move was a question whose answer was no, and that is the point - the reason for not using a plain loop is the most useful artefact this decision produces. Case 2's team cannot use the framework this case lands on, for one reason that has nothing to do with the problem.

plain: Symptom 2: four Python engineers, none with production framework experience, six weeks to ship. Before choosing between frameworks, what is the question - and what in symptom 1 makes the answer harder than it looks?
The prior question is whether you need any of them. Read what happens when you answer yes too quickly, and also what happens when you answer no and the problem turns out to need pausing for days.
A Plain SDK Loop. Its first pitfall - rebuilding a framework badly, one feature at a time - is what symptom 1 would force you into.
langgraph: Symptom 1: cases last three to ten days, a credit officer must approve before anything is sent, and servers are redeployed several times a week. Symptom 4: a restart re-sends a reminder that already went out. What single property is required?
The case has to survive the process that is running it, pause for a human, and resume without repeating what it already did. That last clause is a specific pitfall about where side effects sit.
LangGraph. Read all three pitfalls: the in-memory checkpointer in production, graphs more complex than the problem, and side effects that repeat on resume - symptom 4 is the third one.
pydantic: Symptom 3 has two halves: every outbound message must be a validated structured object, and the board wants the ability to change model provider within a quarter. What single choice serves both?
A typed, validated, model-agnostic layer. Note the caution about what validation does and does not prove, and where case state should live.
Pydantic AI. Read the pitfall about assuming validation means correct values, and the one about putting business state in globals instead of deps.

drop.openai: The OpenAI Agents SDK suits triage-and-specialist designs with handoffs. How many agents does this case need - and how does a provider's own SDK sit with the board policy in symptom 3?
drop.adk: The Google ADK suits Google Cloud, Gemini, and Java or Go shops with A2A needs. What does symptom 2 say the team is?
drop.crew: Role-based agent teams suit work with genuinely separable roles. Read the vendor's six roles in the brief against symptom 1 - how many separable streams of work are there in one collection case?
drop.tsagents: The TypeScript agent stacks put an agent next to a web app. What language does this team write, and where would the agent live?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now notice that one of them is not a framework but a question - and that answering it explicitly is what stops the team from building a graph more complicated than the case, or hand-rolling checkpoints they should not.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Four engineers new to frameworks with six weeks to ship should ask whether a framework is needed at all - and here answer no, for a reason worth writing down.
Ten-day cases with a human approval across weekly redeploys require durable checkpointing, which settles the framework choice immediately.
The board's provider-portability rule and the validated-message requirement both point at one typed, model-agnostic layer.
whyFirst.why: Order by the decision that justifies the others. Durable execution is the requirement that picks the framework and it is your second step - but a team that skips the question tends to adopt more machinery than the problem needs, and the written reason is what lets the next, simpler agent be built with a loop. Asking also surfaces the specific thing you would otherwise hand-roll badly: pause and resume across a redeploy.

cases.title: The agent that keeps being killed mid-task
cases.brief: A B2B SaaS company has put an agent inside its Next.js product: it reads a customer's account, proposes a configuration change, and applies it once an administrator approves. The team is five TypeScript engineers with no Python. The agent streams its reasoning into the UI, which customers like. What they do not like is that it often stops halfway.
evidence: The agent runs inside a Next.js serverless route with a sixty-second timeout. About 23% of runs are killed mid-task.
The approval step waits for an administrator who may take hours, and the HTTP request is held open for it. A redeploy loses the run entirely.
Five TypeScript engineers, no Python. The product streams chat and renders generative UI in the browser, and the team wants to switch model providers freely.
Zod validates the tool arguments and the team treats that as proof the values are right. A well-formed but non-existent account ID was accepted and acted on.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.tsagents: Start here, because three of the four symptoms are this stack's documented failure modes and the team's language rules everything else out. Running a long agent loop inside a serverless request with a short timeout is the first pitfall - 23% killed at sixty seconds. Blocking a request for an approval that may take hours is the second. And trusting Zod as proof that arguments are correct is the third: a well-formed account ID that does not exist validates perfectly. Keep the streaming and generative UI, which this stack is genuinely good at, and move the loop out of the request.
why.plain: Essential here in a way it was not in Case 1: the fix is a plain agent loop in a durable background worker with a job record, not inside the HTTP request. The approval becomes a stored state the administrator resolves later, and the UI subscribes to progress rather than holding a socket open for hours. Mind the pitfalls - set a step budget, and never block a web request on a human.
why.langgraph: Useful as the pattern to copy rather than the tool to adopt: it is the reference design for pause, resume and replay, and this problem is exactly what it solves. It is Python, and the team has none - so take the shape, or run it as a separate service only if the pause-and-resume logic grows beyond a job table. Note how a single fact about the team, not about the problem, moves this from essential in Case 1 to useful here.
why.pydantic: Useful as the same lesson in the other language: validation proves shape, not truth. Whatever validates here, Zod or otherwise, needs a business-rule check behind it that confirms the account exists and belongs to this customer.
why.openai: Useful if the design grows into triage-and-specialist handoffs with guardrails, which it has not yet. Weigh it against the stated wish to switch providers freely.
why.claude: Not needed: it is for agents working with files, code and shells, and this agent changes a SaaS configuration through an API. Nothing here reads a repository.
why.adk: Not needed: no Google Cloud or Gemini requirement, and a TypeScript team gains nothing from a multi-language toolkit.
why.crew: Not needed: one agent, one approval, one configuration change. Role-based teams would add multi-agent cost to a single-agent problem.
why.llamaindex: Not needed: there is no document corpus here, and it would also be the wrong language for this team.

firstWhy.plain: Correct about the destination - a plain loop in a background worker is where this lands - and your second step. But what tells you that is reading the stack's own constraints: the serverless timeout, the held-open request, the Zod assumption. Diagnose with the stack you are on, then restructure.
firstWhy.langgraph: The right pattern for a run that pauses for hours and survives a redeploy, and the honest reason it is not your answer has nothing to do with the problem: it is Python and the team has none. Adopting it would mean a second language and a second deployment for five engineers already shipping a product.
firstWhy.openai: Guardrails and traces out of the box are attractive, and the handoff model may suit you later. But nothing here is a triage problem, and the team has asked to switch providers freely - which is an odd thing to buy a provider's SDK for.

cases.model: Start with the TypeScript agent stack's own guidance, because three of the four symptoms are its named pitfalls: a long agent loop inside a serverless route with a sixty-second timeout kills 23% of runs, holding an HTTP request open for an approval that may take hours is the second, and treating Zod validation as proof the arguments are correct is the third - a well-formed but non-existent account ID passed straight through. Keep what this stack is good at, the streamed reasoning and generative UI customers like. Then restructure around a plain agent loop in a durable background worker with a job record: the run survives a redeploy, the approval becomes stored state an administrator resolves whenever they get to it, and the UI subscribes to progress instead of holding a connection. Give it a step budget. Add a business-rule check behind the schema validation so an account must exist and belong to this customer. Treat LangGraph as the reference design for pause, resume and replay rather than something to adopt - it is Python, and the team has none - and revisit a separate service only if that logic outgrows a job table. The Claude SDK, ADK, role-based crews and LlamaIndex all address problems this product does not have.
cases.note: LangGraph was essential in Case 1 and is only useful here, and the deciding fact is that the team writes TypeScript - nothing about the problem changed. Framework choices are made of team facts as much as requirements.

tsagents: Symptoms 1, 3 and 4 are all about the same stack: a sixty-second serverless timeout killing a quarter of runs, a TypeScript team streaming generative UI, and Zod validation being mistaken for correctness. Where does the guidance for all three live?
The agent is embedded in a web app, which is a specific context with specific traps - about where the loop runs, about waiting for humans, and about what a schema actually proves.
TypeScript Agents: Vercel AI SDK and Mastra. All three pitfalls are in this evidence: long loops in a short-timeout serverless request, blocking on a human approval, and trusting Zod as proof.
plain: Symptom 2: an approval that may take hours, with the HTTP request held open for it, and a redeploy losing the run. If the heavy framework for this is in a language the team does not write - what is the smallest structure that solves it?

Move the loop out of the request into something that runs in the background and records its state, so the approval is data rather than a held connection. There are two pitfalls to respect while doing it.
A Plain SDK Loop. Read the pitfalls about having no step budget and about blocking a web request while waiting for a human.

drop.claude: The Claude Agent SDK suits agents that read and write files, run code or use a shell. What does this agent actually change?
drop.adk: The Google ADK suits Google Cloud, Gemini and multi-language shops. What does symptom 3 say about this team?
drop.crew: Role-based agent teams need genuinely separable roles. How many separable streams of work are there in “propose a config change and apply it on approval”?
drop.llamaindex: LlamaIndex is for agents that are mostly about your documents. What document collection appears in this evidence - and what language is this team?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right, and one obvious candidate is ruled out by a fact about the team rather than the problem. Start by reading the pitfalls of the stack you are already standing on - three of the four symptoms are listed there.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A background worker with a job record is the structure this needs, since the approval may take hours and a redeploy must not lose the run.
Three of the four symptoms are documented pitfalls of the TypeScript agent stack this product already uses, including the timeout and the Zod assumption.
LangGraph solves pause-and-resume properly, so the real question is whether to take on a Python service.
whyFirst.why: Order by where the diagnosis comes from. The background worker is the right destination and is your second step - but what tells you to go there, and what catches the quieter bug, is the stack's own list of traps: the loop in a short-timeout request, the blocked human approval, and Zod mistaken for truth. That third one is silently acting on accounts that do not exist, and no amount of restructuring would have found it.

cases.title: The agent that is really a retrieval project
cases.brief: An insurer's compliance team wants an assistant that answers questions about policy wordings, endorsements and regulator circulars - 400,000 pages of messy PDFs. A vendor has pitched a five-agent crew: researcher, analyst, compliance officer, writer and a manager, each with a role-play prompt. The team is Python, the answers are needed in seconds behind a web request, and nothing is approved, scheduled or paid.
evidence: 95% of what the assistant does is answer questions over the 400,000 pages. Default chunking and top-k have never been tuned, and complex multi-column PDFs retrieve badly.
The team upgraded across minor versions without pinning and the retrieval API moved, breaking the build twice in a month.
The vendor's five roles all need the same documents for every question - there is no separable work, and the roles are expressed as personas rather than tasks.
The assistant has no tools beyond retrieval, no approvals, no long-running cases, and must answer inside a synchronous web request in seconds.
Answers must come back as a structured object - finding, clause citations, confidence - and today the team parses them out of prose with regular expressions.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.llamaindex: Start here, because 95% of the work is retrieval over 400,000 messy pages and that is where the quality lives. Its own pitfalls are both present: default chunking and top-k left untuned on complex PDFs is the first, and upgrading across versions without pinning is the third - which has already broken the build twice. Tune the chunking for multi-column layouts, tune top-k against a real question set, and pin the version.
why.plain: A plain loop is the right structure and the answer to the vendor: no tools beyond retrieval, no approvals, no long-running cases, and a synchronous response needed in seconds. LlamaIndex's own second pitfall is the same point - using a framework's agent layer when a plain loop plus its retrievers would do. Set a step budget and keep it boring.
why.pydantic: The required output is a typed object - finding, clause citations, confidence - and it is currently being scraped out of prose with regular expressions, which fails silently and often. Define the schema and have the model fill it, while remembering that a validated citation can still point at the wrong clause: validation proves shape, not truth.
why.langgraph: Useful if this grows into something with approvals or multi-day reviews, which it is explicitly not today. Adopting a graph framework for a synchronous question-and-answer path would be a graph more complex than the problem.
why.openai: Useful only as a comparison point for guardrails and traces. There is no triage-and-specialist structure here to hand off between.
why.claude: Not needed: it suits agents that read and write files, run code or use a shell, and this one reads an index and answers a question.
why.adk: Not needed: a Python team with no Google Cloud, Gemini, multi-language or A2A requirement.
why.crew: Not needed, and this is the pitch to refuse with reasons. The five roles all need the same documents for every question, so there is no separable work; the roles are personas rather than tasks, which is the first pitfall; and it is multi-agent cost for a single-agent problem, which is the third. Five agents would also make a seconds-level latency budget impossible.
why.tsagents: Not needed: a Python team, and no web product for the agent to live inside.

firstWhy.plain: Right about the structure, right to refuse the crew, and your second step. But structure is not where this assistant will succeed or fail: 95% of the work is retrieval over 400,000 messy pages, and a beautifully simple loop over untuned chunking still answers badly.
firstWhy.pydantic: The regex parsing is genuinely fragile and the typed output is required, so this is real work. It is also the last mile - a perfectly typed object containing a wrong finding, retrieved from a badly chunked multi-column PDF, is worse than prose, because it looks authoritative.
firstWhy.langgraph: Reasonable if you expect approvals and multi-day reviews later. But symptom 4 says plainly that there are none today, and a graph for a synchronous question-and-answer path is the definition of machinery exceeding the problem.

cases.model: Start with the document layer, because 95% of this assistant is retrieval over 400,000 messy pages and that is where the answer quality is decided: tune chunking for complex multi-column PDFs rather than leaving the defaults, tune top-k against a real question set, and pin the version, since upgrading across minor releases without pinning has already broken the build twice. Then build the agent as a plain loop with a step budget - no tools beyond retrieval, no approvals, no long-running cases, and a synchronous response in seconds, which is precisely when a framework's agent layer is the wrong purchase. Then define the output as a typed object with finding, clause citations and confidence, replacing the regular-expression parsing, while remembering that a validated citation can still point at the wrong clause. Keep LangGraph in reserve for the day approvals or multi-day reviews appear. Refuse the five-agent crew explicitly: the roles are personas rather than tasks, they all need the same documents for every question so there is nothing separable to parallelise, and five agents would make a seconds-level latency budget unreachable.
cases.note: Across the three cases the first move was set by whichever part of the system the work actually lived in - the ten-day case, the embedded web stack, the document corpus - and twice the right answer included refusing a vendor's multi-agent pitch. The framework question is usually the second question.

llamaindex: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together: 95% of the work is answering over 400,000 messy pages, default chunking and top-k are untuned, complex multi-column PDFs retrieve badly, and unpinned upgrades have broken the build twice. What kind of project is this?
Mostly a documents project. The framework to look at is the one built for that - and two of its three pitfalls are sitting in this evidence already.
LlamaIndex. Read the pitfall about default chunking and top-k left untuned on complex PDFs, and the one about upgrading across versions without pinning.
plain: Symptom 4: no tools beyond retrieval, no approvals, no long-running cases, and an answer needed inside a synchronous web request. Symptom 3: a vendor wants five role-played agents. What is the right amount of machinery?
The smallest thing that works. One of the document framework's own pitfalls makes the same point about its agent layer - and there are two things you still must not forget to add.
A Plain SDK Loop. Note the pitfalls about having no step budget and about rebuilding a framework badly - then read LlamaIndex's second pitfall alongside it.
pydantic: Symptom 5: the answer must be a structured object - finding, clause citations, confidence - and today it is pulled out of prose with regular expressions. What replaces that, and what must you not conclude from it?
Have the model produce the typed object directly, validated. But validation tells you the shape is right, not that the clause cited actually says what the finding claims.
Pydantic AI. Read the pitfall about assuming validation means correct values.

drop.adk: The Google ADK suits Google Cloud, Gemini and Java or Go teams with A2A needs. What does the brief say the team is?
drop.crew: Role-based agent teams need separable roles. Read symptom 3: how many of the five roles need the same documents for every question - and what would five agents do to a seconds-level latency budget?
drop.tsagents: The TypeScript stacks embed an agent beside a web app. What language is this team, and what product would it be embedded in?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now weigh them by where the quality comes from: two of your choices shape how the assistant is built, and one decides whether it finds the right clause in 400,000 pages.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 95% of the work is retrieval over 400,000 messy pages with untuned chunking, so that is where answer quality is decided.
There are no tools, approvals or long-running cases, so a plain loop is right and the five-agent crew must be refused.
The required typed output is currently being scraped out of prose with regular expressions, which fails silently.
whyFirst.why: Order by where the quality lives. The plain loop is the right structure and refusing the crew matters, and the typed output must be fixed - but a simple loop over badly chunked multi-column PDFs still returns the wrong clause, and a perfectly validated object containing a wrong finding is more dangerous than prose, because it reads as authoritative. Tune the retrieval first; it is 95% of what this thing does.

plain.t: A plain agent loop is 30 lines. Later you add retries (about 40 lines), saving and restoring state (about 150), pausing for approval and resuming (about 120) and tracing (about 60). How many lines do you now maintain?
plain.a: 30 + 40 + 150 + 120 + 60 = 400 lines, most of them the durability features a framework such as LangGraph or Pydantic AI with Temporal provides. That is the signal to adopt one for this agent, not before.
iv: When would you not use an agent framework?

When the agent is a simple tool loop with a few tools, short runs and no need to pause and resume. A provider SDK loop is small, transparent and has no framework upgrades to track. Adopt a framework when a concrete need appears, such as durable state, human approvals that take hours, or multi-agent orchestration.
What must a hand-written loop always have?

A step budget so it cannot run forever, clear tool schemas, error handling that returns failures to the model rather than crashing, an approval gate before risky actions, and tracing so you can see what happened.
mis: Adopting a framework for a two-tool agent
Start with the loop; add a framework for a real need
Re-implementing durability by hand
Adopt durable execution when runs get long

pydantic.t: An agent’s output fails validation 8% of the time on the first try. Pydantic AI sends the error back, and each retry succeeds 75% of the time. With two retries, what share of runs still fails validation, in percent?
pydantic.a: 0.08 × 0.25 × 0.25 = 0.005, or 0.5%. Validation plus retries catches most shape errors; the remaining failures need handling, and valid shape still does not guarantee correct values.
iv: What does Pydantic AI add over a plain SDK?

Typed agents: an output type that the answer must validate against, with automatic retries when it does not; typed tool arguments; dependency injection so tools get a bank client or database that tests can replace; one API across providers; and integrations for durable execution, tracing and evals.
Why inject dependencies into an agent?
So tools do not reach for globals. Passing a typed dependency such as a bank client makes the agent testable with a fake, keeps credentials out of prompts, and makes it clear what each run can touch.
mis: Treating validated output as correct
Check values with business rules (Prompting & Structured Outputs)
Globals inside tools
Inject dependencies through deps

langgraph.t: A 10-step agent run takes 40 seconds per step and crashes at step 7. Without a checkpointer it restarts from step 1; with one it redoes only step 7. How many seconds of work does the checkpointer save?
langgraph.a: Without it, steps 1 to 7 run again: 280 seconds. With it, only step 7: 40 seconds. It saves 240 seconds, plus the model cost of six steps, and it avoids repeating side effects that already happened.
iv: How does LangGraph support human-in-the-loop?

A node calls interrupt() with the data a human needs. The run stops, its state is saved by the checkpointer under a thread id, and it can be resumed later, from any process, with Command(resume=...). Because state is persisted, the wait can be hours or days.
What is the catch with resuming after an interrupt?

The interrupted node runs again from its start when resumed, so code before interrupt() executes twice. Put side effects after the interrupt and make them idempotent, and use a persistent checkpointer such as Postgres rather than the in-memory one in production.
mis: In-memory checkpointer in production
Use Postgres or another persistent store
Side effects before interrupt()
Place them after the approval, and make them idempotent

openai.t: A triage agent on a small model costs ₹0.05 per chat and handles 100,000 chats a day, handing off 30% to a specialist that costs ₹0.60 per chat. What is the daily cost, in ₹?
openai.a: 100,000 × ₹0.05 = ₹5,000 for triage, plus 30,000 × ₹0.60 = ₹18,000 for the specialist: ₹23,000 a day, against ₹60,000 if every chat went to the specialist. The handoff rate, visible in traces, drives the bill.
iv: What is the difference between a handoff and calling an agent as a tool?

A handoff transfers the conversation to another agent, which then talks to the user directly. Calling an agent as a tool keeps the first agent in charge; it gets the sub-agent’s result back and continues. Use handoffs for routing to specialists and agents-as-tools for sub-tasks.
What are guardrails in the OpenAI Agents SDK?

Checks that run on the input to the first agent or the output of the last, alongside the agent. If one trips, the run stops with an exception. They are useful for cheap policy checks, but they are one layer, not the whole safety design (Guardrails).
mis: Agents bouncing handoffs back and forth
Give each agent a clear remit and a limit
Guardrails as the only safety layer
Combine with tool permissions and approval gates

claude.t: An agent runs 50 tasks a day with 12 tool calls each. If every call needed a manual approval, how many approvals would that be? If only the one dispute-raising call per task is gated, how many approvals a day?
claude.a: 12 × 50 = 600 approvals a day if everything is gated, which nobody will review properly. Allowing read-only tools and gating only the risky call gives 50: a number people can actually review.
iv: When is the Claude Agent SDK a better fit than a lighter framework?

When the agent needs a workspace: reading and writing files, running scripts or shell commands, browsing, and managing long contexts, as in operations, research or coding tasks. It gives you the Claude Code harness with those tools, subagents, sessions and hooks. For a two-tool chat agent it is more than you need.
How do you keep an autonomous agent with shell access safe?

Allow only the tools the task needs, gate risky ones with PreToolUse hooks or approval, avoid bypass-permissions mode outside a sandbox, run in a container with no production credentials, cap turns, and log every tool call (Agent Security).
mis: Granting Bash and write access by default
Allow only what the task needs
Gating every call
Gate the risky ones so reviews stay meaningful

adk.t: Three independent verification checks take 4, 6 and 5 seconds. How many seconds does running them in a ParallelAgent save compared with a SequentialAgent?
adk.a: Sequentially they take 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 seconds; in parallel the slowest decides, 6 seconds. That saves 9 seconds per case, provided the checks really are independent.
iv: What are workflow agents in ADK?

Agents that orchestrate other agents without calling a model themselves: a SequentialAgent runs sub-agents in order, a ParallelAgent runs them at once, and a LoopAgent repeats until a condition is met. They give deterministic structure around LLM agents that decide within each step.
Why might a bank choose ADK?

If it runs on Google Cloud or uses Gemini, or its engineers work in Java or Go, since ADK supports Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin. Built-in evaluation, a development UI and A2A support help too. Feature parity varies by language, so check the features you need in yours.
mis: Parallel agents that share mutable state
Parallelise only independent checks
Assuming identical features in every language
Check the docs for your language

crew.t: A single agent handles a support case with about 10,000 tokens. A two-agent crew uses 4 exchanges of about 9,000 tokens each. How many times the tokens does the crew use?
crew.a: 4 × 9,000 = 36,000 tokens against 10,000: 3.6 times. If accuracy does not improve, the crew is pure overhead. Multi-agent designs pay off only when work is genuinely separable or parallel (Multi-Agent Systems).
iv: What happened to AutoGen?

Microsoft moved AutoGen to maintenance mode in October 2025, with only critical fixes. Its successor, Microsoft Agent Framework, reached 1.0 in April 2026 and merges AutoGen’s agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel’s enterprise features for .NET and Python. AG2 continues AutoGen as a community project. New work should not start on AutoGen.
When would you pick CrewAI?

When the work divides naturally into roles with clear hand-offs, such as research, analysis and writing, and you want a quick, readable way to express that in Python. Use Flows for state and control around crews, start with a sequential process, and compare cost and consistency against a single agent.
mis: Starting new projects on AutoGen
Use Microsoft Agent Framework or another maintained option
A crew for a single-agent task
Measure against one agent first

tsagents.t: An agent route uses stopWhen: stepCountIs(8) and each step averages 1.2 s. What is the worst-case time in seconds before the step limit stops it?
tsagents.a: 8 × 1.2 = 9.6 s, close to common serverless limits; long cases belong in a workflow that can suspend.
iv: How would you build an agent inside a Next.js product?

Use the Vercel AI SDK: tools with Zod schemas, streamText with a step limit in a route handler, and useChat in the UI. Move approvals that take hours into a Mastra or LangGraph.js workflow that suspends and resumes.
Why not block a request waiting for a human?
Serverless requests time out and hold resources; suspend the run, store state and resume when the reviewer answers.
mis: Long loops inside a short serverless request
Bound the steps, or run in a worker or workflow
Blocking on human approval
Suspend and resume from storage

llamaindex.t: A query engine returns 4 chunks of 512 tokens, and the system prompt plus question are 1,200 tokens. How many input tokens per rules lookup?
iv: When would you pick LlamaIndex over other agent frameworks?
When the agent’s work is mostly about documents: loading, parsing, indexing and querying many sources. Its query engines become tools, and Workflows add resumable steps.
How does a LlamaIndex agent keep state across a long case?
Run it with a Context, serialise it with to_dict, store it, and restore with Context.from_dict to resume.
mis: Leaving default chunking and top-k on complex PDFs
Tune parsing, chunking and top-k with evals
Not pinning versions
Pin and upgrade deliberately

gloss: agent loop
Call the model with tools, run the tools it requests, return the results, and repeat until it answers.
step budget
A cap on loop iterations or tool calls so an agent cannot run forever.
framework lock-in
Depending on a framework’s abstractions so deeply that switching is costly.
output type
In Pydantic AI, the typed model an agent’s final answer must validate against.
dependency injection
Passing resources such as a database client into an agent run instead of using globals.
checkpointer
LangGraph’s store that saves graph state after each step, per thread.
thread
One saved conversation or case history that a run can pause and resume.
interrupt
A LangGraph call that pauses a run for human input until it is resumed.
handoff
Transferring a conversation to another agent that then answers the user directly.
tripwire
A guardrail result that stops an agent run immediately.
hook
Code that runs at a point in the agent loop, such as before a tool call, and can block it.
workflow agent
In ADK, an agent that orchestrates sub-agents in sequence, in parallel or in a loop.
crew
In CrewAI, a set of role-based agents working through tasks under a process.
durable execution
Running long workflows so they survive crashes and resume from saved state.
Zod
A TypeScript schema library used to define and validate tool inputs.
streamText
AI SDK function that runs the tool loop and streams tokens and tool calls.
query engine
A LlamaIndex object that retrieves and synthesises an answer from an index.
QueryEngineTool
A wrapper that lets an agent call a query engine as a tool.

plain.note: A plain SDK loop is the ReAct pattern written by hand: reason, call a tool, observe, repeat.

plain.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
plain.note: MCP lets tools written once be used from a plain loop or any framework, which reduces lock-in.

langgraph.name: Durable Execution and Checkpointing
langgraph.note: LangGraph’s checkpointer is one way to get the durable execution that long agent runs need.

langgraph.name: TypeScript Agents: Vercel AI SDK and Mastra
langgraph.note: LangGraph.js is the durable alternative when TypeScript runs must checkpoint for days.

crew.name: Single vs Multi-Agent
crew.note: Choose a multi-agent framework only after checking that the work really needs several agents.

openai.name: Output Guardrails
openai.note: Agents SDK guardrails are one implementation of input and output rails, not a complete safety layer.

claude.name: Sandboxing and Egress Control
claude.note: An agent with shell and file tools must run in a sandbox with narrow permissions.

adk.name: Agent-to-Agent Protocols (A2A)
adk.note: ADK speaks A2A, so its agents can call and be called by agents built with other frameworks.

pydantic.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
pydantic.note: Pydantic AI’s output types are strict structured outputs with a validation-and-retry loop built in.

tsagents.name: LangGraph
tsagents.note: LangGraph.js is the durable alternative when TypeScript runs must checkpoint for days.

tsagents.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
tsagents.note: Streaming with streamText and useChat is how TypeScript apps meet latency budgets.

llamaindex.name: Document Parsing and OCR
llamaindex.note: LlamaParse and readers handle the parsing step of a RAG pipeline.

llamaindex.name: Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders
llamaindex.note: Query engines can include re-rankers before the agent sees results.
